title: Captain Whitfield and John Manjiro
text:
In January 1841 a fourteen year old fisherman's boy named Manjiro and four companions were blown out to sea off the coast of Tosa, in Japan. They were wrecked on the uninhabited island of Torishima and survived for months on birds and rainwater. In June an American whaling ship, the John Howland, captained by William Whitfield of Fairhaven, Massachusetts, spotted them and took them aboard.

Japan was then closed to the outside world, and returning castaways risked death. Whitfield left the older men in Hawaii, but Manjiro, bright and curious, wanted to go with him. The captain took him home to Fairhaven, treated him as a son, and sent him to school, where he learned English, mathematics and navigation. The boy, called John Mung by the Americans, later sailed on whalers himself and earned money in the California Gold Rush.

In 1851 he managed to return to Japan. After long questioning by officials he was made a samurai and became a valued interpreter and teacher of English and navigation, helping Japan in its first dealings with the United States. His and Whitfield's descendants kept in touch for generations.
lesson: Kindness to a stranger far from home can change a life and build bridges far beyond it. Treat the outsider in your care as you would your own.
location: Torishima, Japan, and Fairhaven, Massachusetts, USA
source: Manjiro's account to Japanese officials (Hyoson Kiryaku, 1852); Emily V. Warinner, Voyager to Destiny (1956)
